# Mechanical calculator (`mechanical_calculator`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: needs gears_gear_trains; helped by arabic_numerals, mechanical_clock, lathe_screw_cutting, interchangeable_parts, logarithms
- Core idea: Each decimal place is a wheel with ten positions. Adding a digit turns the wheel by that many steps; when a wheel passes from 9 to 0 a tooth or lever pushes the next wheel on by one, which is the carry and the hard part. Subtraction is done by turning backwards or by adding the nines' complement. Multiplication is repeated addition with a shift: Leibniz's stepped drum, a cylinder with nine teeth of graded length, lets one set a number once and add it with each turn of a crank, and a sliding carriage moves it one place for the next digit. A machine that works reliably needs parts as accurate as a good clock.
- Pitfalls:
  - A carry that needs the force of the user's hand to ripple through many wheels: 999,999 + 1 jams; the carry must store energy or act one wheel after another
  - Wheels without a detent that overshoot or stop between digits
  - Thinking that it speeds up all arithmetic; before the 1850s logarithm tables and trained human computers were faster and cheaper
  - Calling the Antikythera mechanism or the abacus a calculator of this kind; the first is a geared model of the heavens, the second has no automatic carry
- History: greece: c. 2nd–1st c. BC – Antikythera mechanism, a geared astronomical calculator; europe: 1623 – Schickard's calculating clock (known from letters to Kepler; the machine was lost); 1642–1645 Pascal's adding machine, surviving models include machines with separate wheels for livres, sols and deniers; 1673 Leibniz shows a model of the stepped reckoner, working machine c. 1694; 1820 Thomas de Colmar's arithmometer, in series production from 1851; 1870s Odhner's pinwheel machine; americas: 1887 – Felt's key-driven Comptometer; 1888–1892 Burroughs's printing adding machine
- Read:
  - Michael R. Williams, A History of Computing Technology (1985)
  - Matthew L. Jones, Reckoning with Matter: Calculating Machines, Innovation, and Thinking about Thinking from Pascal to Babbage (2016)
